facts.claim: Franklin's self-improvement plan tracked thirteen virtues.
facts.mechanism: Because A finite list made faults observable and allowed focused practice instead of an undifferentiated demand for perfection.
facts.commonError: Franklin used a ten-commandment-style list of prohibitions.
facts.whyWrong: His plan contained thirteen positive and restraining dispositions with practical definitions.

facts.claim: Franklin emphasized one virtue per week while continuing to mark faults against all thirteen.
facts.mechanism: Because Concentrated attention reduced overload while the full chart preserved accountability across the set.
facts.commonError: He attempted to perfect all thirteen with equal attention every day.
facts.whyWrong: The rotating weekly emphasis was central to the design.

facts.claim: A thirteen-week rotation can be completed four times in a fifty-two-week year.
facts.mechanism: Because Thirteen multiplied by four equals fifty-two, giving the practice a repeatable annual cycle.
facts.commonError: Each virtue received attention only once in a year.
facts.whyWrong: The cycle was designed to repeat four times.

facts.claim: Aristotle's ethical mean is relative to the person and situation rather than an arithmetic midpoint.
facts.mechanism: Because Appropriate action depends on circumstances, motives, objects, timing, and manner as judged by practical wisdom.
facts.commonError: Virtue always means choosing the numerically moderate option.
facts.whyWrong: Some situations require intense or decisive action, and the mean concerns fitting response rather than quantity alone.

facts.claim: Aristotelian eudaimonia concerns activity across a complete life, not a passing pleasant mood.
facts.mechanism: Because Flourishing evaluates how capacities and relationships are exercised over time under real conditions.
facts.commonError: Ancient happiness is simply the same feeling measured by a momentary mood scale.
facts.whyWrong: Eudaimonia is a judgment about living and functioning well, not only affect.

facts.claim: Kant's categorical imperative tests whether a maxim can be willed as a universal law.
facts.mechanism: Because Universalization blocks making a private exception for oneself while expecting others to follow a different rule.
facts.commonError: Kantian ethics asks which act produces the greatest total happiness.
facts.whyWrong: Aggregate welfare is a utilitarian criterion associated with Bentham, not Kant's duty test.

facts.claim: Benthamite utilitarianism evaluates actions by their consequences for aggregate pleasure and pain.
facts.mechanism: Because It treats each affected person's welfare as part of the outcome to be compared.
facts.commonError: Utilitarianism defines morality as faithful adherence to inherited character roles.
facts.whyWrong: Its criterion is consequence, not tradition or role excellence.

facts.claim: The VIA classification contains twenty-four character strengths grouped under six broad virtue categories.
facts.mechanism: Because Specific measurable traits provide behavioral routes through which broader virtues can be expressed.
facts.commonError: The VIA system consists of six strengths total.
facts.whyWrong: Six is the number of umbrella virtues; the inventory names twenty-four strengths.

facts.claim: The six VIA virtue categories are wisdom, courage, humanity, justice, temperance, and transcendence.
facts.mechanism: Because The categories cluster cognitive, emotional, interpersonal, civic, restraining, and meaning-oriented strengths.
facts.commonError: The VIA's six virtues are identical to Franklin's first six entries.
facts.whyWrong: The VIA taxonomy was a separate cross-tradition project with different groupings.
